# Tides and tide tables (`tides_tide_tables`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by universal_gravitation, sounding_lead_pilotage
- Core idea: At a port with predominantly semidiurnal tides, successive high waters are about 12 hours 25 minutes apart on average. Other ports have one high water a day or two of unequal height. The Moon and Sun both contribute tidal forces. Around new and full moon their effects reinforce one another, giving spring tides. Near the quarters the range is usually smaller. The shape and depth of a basin affect both height and timing. Repeated local observations establish a port's usual delay after lunar transit and the variation through the lunar month. A rough harbour table is possible centuries before a gravitational theory. Many Mediterranean ports have a small range, whereas the Bay of Fundy can reach about 16 m.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating Mediterranean experience as valid outside; Italian crews get caught out on Atlantic and Channel coasts
  - Inferring the number or timing of local tides directly from the Moon overhead; basins respond differently
  - Applying one port's timing to another harbour along the coast
- History: greece: c. 325 BC – Pytheas links tides to the Moon; 2nd c. BC Seleucus notes the daily inequality; china: c. 770 – Dou Shumeng describes a graphical method for predicting tides; surviving Qiantang tables date to AD 1056; islamic: c. 850 – Abu Ma'shar discusses tides and the Moon; europe: 725 – Bede notes that high water comes at different times at different ports; 13th c. tide table 'flod at London brigge'; 1687 Newton's gravitational explanation; 1872 Kelvin's tide-predicting machine
- Read:
  - Bede, De temporum ratione (725), ch. 29
  - Yang Zuosheng et al., Historical Development and Use of Thousand-Year-Old Tide-Prediction Tables, Limnology and Oceanography 34 (1989), 953–957
  - David Edgar Cartwright, Tides: A Scientific History (1999)
